title: Three baskets
hook: discipline, discourses, and the higher teaching: the Pali canon

segments.voice: Yesterday: Theravada, and your line, the way of the elders. Did you do one thing an elder taught you, on purpose? Day two hundred ninety-two.

In Mandalay, in Myanmar, there's a pagoda surrounded by hundreds of small white shrines, row after row, like a quiet city. Inside each one stands a marble slab, taller than a person, carved on both sides with tiny letters. Walk them all and you've walked through a book. In the nineteenth century, a Burmese king had the entire Buddhist scripture of his tradition carved in stone, seven hundred twenty-nine slabs, so it would outlast palm leaves and paper. People call it the world's largest book. What's carved on those slabs comes in three parts. Today: the three baskets.
screen: `A CITY OF WHITE SHRINES.` → `MARBLE SLABS, BOTH SIDES CARVED.` → `THE WORLD'S LARGEST BOOK.`

segments.voice: Tipitaka. Ti, three. Piṭaka, basket. The three baskets. Nobody is completely sure why baskets. One old explanation pictures workers on a building site, passing baskets of earth from hand to hand down a line, the way the teaching was passed down from teacher to student by memory for centuries before it was written. The first basket is the Vinaya, the discipline. It holds the rules for monks and nuns, and, charmingly, the story behind almost every rule: what happened that made the Buddha say, from now on, don't do that. The second basket is the Suttas, the discourses: the Buddha's talks and conversations, gathered into five collections, the long ones, the middle-length ones, the connected ones grouped by topic, the numbered ones grouped by how many items they list, and a fifth collection of shorter works. That fifth one holds the Dhammapada, which this path walked through verse by verse. One of its most loved verses sums up the whole in Max Müller's English: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." The third basket is the Abhidhamma, the higher teaching: seven books that analyze the mind and experience into their tiniest moments, like a chemistry of consciousness. Theravada Buddhists study it seriously, and in Myanmar it's especially honored. Printed, the three baskets fill dozens of volumes. In 1881 a British scholar, T. W. Rhys Davids, founded a society to publish and translate them, and many English versions quoted on this path come from that effort.
screen: `TI: THREE. PIṬAKA: BASKET.` · `VINAYA: THE DISCIPLINE.` · `SUTTAS: THE DISCOURSES.` · `ABHIDHAMMA: THE HIGHER TEACHING.` · then, large: `THREE BASKETS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. On the first breath, name the first basket silently: discipline. How you live. On the second: discourses. What the Buddha taught. On the third: the higher teaching. How the mind works, moment by moment. Then go around again, slowly: discipline, discourses, higher teaching. When they feel familiar, let the names go, and just notice this moment of mind, the one the third basket is trying to describe. The bell holds the time.
Tipitaka. The three baskets of the Pali canon: the discipline, the discourses, and the higher teaching.
Your line: three baskets. Today, notice one moment where how you live, what you've learned, and what your mind is doing all meet. Day two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Theravada monks memorize and chant passages from all three baskets, recite the monastic rules every two weeks, and in Myanmar many monks sit rigorous exams on the whole canon.

fork.setup: you want to know why monks don't eat after noon. which basket do you open?
fork.reveal: the Vinaya holds the monastic rules and the stories of how each came about.

original.note: Pali tipiṭaka: three baskets; Sanskrit tripiṭaka.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Pali canon is one book, like a Bible.
what it means: three baskets: discipline, discourses and the higher teaching, dozens of volumes in print.
what a scholar hears: the Kuthodaw slabs in Mandalay were carved under King Mindon after the 1871 council; the Pali Text Society, founded by Rhys Davids in 1881, still publishes the canon.

notes: Check Müller's exact wording of Dhammapada 183 in SBE 10 (quoted from memory, including the parenthetical '(all)').
Kuthodaw Pagoda: 729 slabs, carving completed 1868 under King Mindon; the 'Fifth Council' was 1871. Confirm dates.
The 'baskets passed hand to hand' explanation of piṭaka is one traditional/scholarly suggestion; presented as uncertain.
